mainTopic: Local custom in farming partnerships (who does which work, what is shared), and a new משנה on rent when a field's spring or trees are lost.
overview: This amud finishes the משנה about a worker who farms another person's field. The owner and worker share the vine branches and poles, and both supply the poles. A ברייתא teaches that the worker must cut or uproot the crop according to local custom, because each side has a real interest and can block a change. The גמרא then explains several lines of the משנה. A worker who weeded on his own must still plow. The word 'הכל' adds that local custom decides whether the trees are part of the deal. In each case, a silent intention does not count, even one backed by a changed share; you have to spell it out at the start. רב יוסף adds the Babylonian custom about straw, and he divides the fencing, tools and irrigation work between the owner and the אריס. A new משנה then rules that a tenant pays full rent when the spring dries up or the trees are cut down, unless he rented the field by name as an irrigated or tree field. רב פפא explains that the case is a small river serving only this field, and his explanation continues on the next amud.

steps.title: End of the משנה: sharing branches and poles
steps.stepSummary: The משנה ends by saying the owner and worker share the vine branches and poles, and both must supply the poles.
steps.simpleTranslation: …in the branches and the poles, and the two of them supply the poles.
steps.whatsHappening: These are the last words of the משנה. Just as the owner and the worker split the wine, they also split the leftover vine branches and the poles, and both of them pay to supply the poles.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's point is that the partnership covers more than the main crop. Side products like branches and poles are shared too. The last clause, that both supply the poles, is explained later in the גמרא (step 25) as the reason the poles are shared.

keyTerms.meaning: poles/reeds used to hold up the vines

phrases.english: in the branches and the poles,
phrases.notes: This picks up in the middle of a sentence. The משנה just said the owner and worker split the wine, and so they also split these.

phrases.english: and the two of them supply the poles.

steps.triggerLanguage: בַּזְּמוֹרוֹת וּבַקָּנִים, וּשְׁנֵיהֶם מְסַפְּקִין אֶת הַקָּנִים
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The owner and the worker share the vine branches and poles, and both supply the poles.

steps.title: A ברייתא: the custom on cutting or uprooting is binding
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rules that the worker must follow local custom on whether to cut or uproot the crop, and that each side can stop the other from changing it.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: It was taught: In a place where they usually cut the crop, he may not uproot it. Where they usually uproot, he may not cut it. And the two of them can block each other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that adds detail to the משנה's rule about following local custom. The worker must harvest the way people in that place usually harvest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two ways to harvest. You can cut the stalks and leave the stubble in the ground, or you can pull out the whole plant. The ברייתא says the local custom decides which one is used, and neither the owner nor the worker can change it alone. The last line, about each side blocking the other, is what the גמרא will ask about soon.

keyTerms.meaning: to cut (the stalks, leaving the roots in the ground)
to uproot (pull out the whole plant)
each one can hold back / block the other

phrases.english: GEMARA: It was taught: In a place where they were accustomed to cut,
he is not permitted to uproot;
where they were accustomed to uproot, he is not permitted to cut;
and the two of them can block each other.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא that adds detail to the משנה's rule of following local custom in a farming partnership.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The harvesting method follows local custom, and each side can prevent the other from changing it.
steps.whatToRemember: Cutting versus uprooting is decided by local custom, not by what either side prefers.

steps.title: Why each side cares about the custom
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains, for each custom, what reason the owner and the worker would each have for objecting to a change.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where the custom is to cut, he may not uproot. This one (the owner) says: 'I want my land fertilized with stubble.' And that one (the worker) says: 'I can't uproot.' Where the custom is to uproot, he may not cut. This one (the owner) says: 'I want my land cleared.' And that one (the worker) says: 'I want the straw.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes through both cases of the ברייתא. For each one, it shows why both the owner and the worker have a fair reason to keep the custom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Where people cut, the owner wants the stubble left in the ground as fertilizer. The worker, on his side, can say uprooting is too much work for him. Where people uproot, the owner wants a clean field. The worker, on his side, wants the straw he gets from pulling out the whole plant. Since each side has something real to lose, neither one can force a change.

keyTerms.meaning: be fertilized by the stubble left behind

steps.confusionAlert: 'הַאי' and 'וְהַאי' mean 'this one' and 'that one.' In each pair, the first is the owner and the second is the worker. Each one explains why he can block a change the other side wants.

phrases.english: Where the custom is to cut, he is not permitted to uproot:

phrases.aramaic: הַאי אָמַר: בָּעֵינָא דְּתִתַּבַּן לִי אַרְעַאי,
phrases.english: this one says: I want my land to be fertilized with stubble;
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the owner. The roots left in the ground after cutting enrich the soil.

phrases.english: and that one says: I am not able.
phrases.notes: 'That one' is the worker. Pulling out every plant is harder work than cutting.

phrases.english: Where the custom is to uproot, he is not permitted to cut:
this one says: I want my land to be cleared;
and that one says: I want the straw.

steps.triggerLanguage: לִקְצוֹר אֵינוֹ רַשַּׁאי לַעֲקוֹר, הַאי אָמַר: בָּעֵינָא דְּתִתַּבַּן לִי אַרְעַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasons behind each case of the ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both owner and worker have a real interest in each harvesting method, so the custom protects both of them.

steps.title: Why does the ברייתא need the last line?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא adds 'the two of them can block each other,' since the cases already showed this.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And the two of them can block each other.' Why do I need this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the last line of the ברייתא and asks what it adds. This question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the ברייתא said the worker may not change from cutting to uprooting or the reverse, we already know the custom holds. So the line saying each side can block the other looks like a needless repeat. The גמרא wants to know its purpose.

keyTerms.meaning: why do I need it? (asks what a line adds)

phrases.english: 'And the two of them can block each other':
why do I need it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּשְׁנֵיהֶם מְעַכְּבִין זֶה עַל זֶה, לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the wording of the ברייתא and questions its final clause.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the clause 'the two of them can block each other' adds beyond the earlier rulings.
steps.kashyaTarget: The final clause of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The clause seems repetitive, since the earlier rulings already make the custom binding.

steps.title: The last line gives the reason
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the last line is not a new rule. It explains why the worker may not change the custom.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is saying 'what is the reason.' What is the reason that where they cut he may not uproot, and where they uproot he may not cut? Because the two of them can block each other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is giving a reason, not a second rule. The worker may not change the custom because each side has the right to stop the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא should be read as one sentence: 'He may not change the custom, because each side can object.' The reasons from step 3 are what give each side that right. So the last line ties the whole ruling together and is not a repeat.

keyTerms.meaning: it is explaining 'what is the reason'

steps.whatToRemember: The rule 'follow the local custom' comes from both sides having rights: each one has a real interest, so either can block a change.

phrases.english: It is saying 'what is the reason':

phrases.aramaic: מַה טַּעַם לִקְצוֹר אֵינוֹ רַשַּׁאי לַעֲקוֹר,
phrases.english: What is the reason that where they cut, he may not uproot,
and where they uproot, he may not cut?

phrases.aramaic: מִשּׁוּם דִּשְׁנֵיהֶם מְעַכְּבִין זֶה עַל זֶה.
phrases.english: Because the two of them can block each other.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the extra clause.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the wording: the clause is the reason for the ruling, not a separate rule.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The clause seemed to be a separate, repeated statement.
steps.terutzMaskana: The clause explains why the custom is binding: each side can object to a change.

steps.title: Why say the worker must plow if that is the custom?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's line that the worker must plow after the harvest where that is the custom, and asks why this needs to be said.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: if the custom is to plow after the harvest, he must plow. Isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a line from the משנה and asks why it needs to be stated at all. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה has just taught that the worker must follow the local custom on cutting or uprooting. So 'if they plow, he must plow' looks like an obvious case of the same idea and seems to add nothing. The question is about why the line is there, not about what the rule is.

keyTerms.meaning: It's obvious! (the גמרא asks why this needs to be said)

phrases.english: If the custom is to plow after the harvest – he must plow.
It is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next line of the משנה after finishing the discussion of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's line 'if the custom is to plow, he must plow'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Following custom has already been taught, so this line seems to repeat it.

steps.title: The worker who weeded instead
steps.stepSummary: The line is needed for a worker who weeded in a place where people don't weed. He might think the weeding frees him from plowing. The משנה teaches that he still has to plow unless he said so in advance.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a place where people do not weed, and this worker went ahead and weeded. You might think he can tell the owner: 'I weeded on the understanding that I would not plow.' So the משנה teaches that he should have said that out loud at the start.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the line covers a worker who did extra work (weeding) and then wants to skip the plowing that is the custom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new point is that a private intention to swap one job for another does not count. The custom still holds unless the worker clearly stated the change when they made the deal.

keyTerms.meaning: No, it is needed for... (introduces the case the line is really about)
to spell it out, to state clearly

steps.confusionAlert: The worker did not refuse to work. He did a different job and assumed it replaced the plowing. The point is that keeping that idea to himself does not change the deal.
steps.whyThisMatters: The rule 'he should have spelled it out' shows up again twice in this סוגיא. Silent intentions don't change a deal set by custom.

phrases.english: No, it is needed: in a place where they do not weed –
and he went and weeded.
You might have said: he can say to him:

phrases.aramaic: הַאי דְּנַכֵּישְׁנָא אַדַּעְתָּא דְּלָא כָּרֵיבְנָא לַהּ,
phrases.english: 'When I weeded, I did it on the understanding that I would not plow it,'

phrases.aramaic: קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן דְּאִיבְּעִי לֵיהּ לְפָרוֹשֵׁי לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: it teaches us that he should have spelled it out to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of why the line is needed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the line a new case where it is not obvious
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A worker who weeded on his own might be excused from plowing because of what he had in mind.
steps.terutzMaskana: He must plow anyway, because he did not state his condition up front.

steps.title: What does the word 'everything' add?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes 'everything follows the custom of the region' and asks what the extra word 'everything' comes to include.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: everything follows the custom of the region. What does the word 'everything' come to include?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא focuses on one word in the משנה, 'הכל', and asks what extra case it adds. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא assumes that a broad word like 'everything' is there to add a case not already mentioned. It is asking what that case is.

phrases.english: Everything follows the custom of the region.
'Everything' – to include what?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to another phrase in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which extra case the word 'הכל' adds.

steps.title: It adds the rule about renting out trees
steps.stepSummary: 'Everything' adds a ברייתא: where the custom is to include the trees when renting out land, they are included; where it is not, they are not.
steps.simpleTranslation: It adds what the Rabbis taught: in a place where the custom is to rent out the trees along with the land, they are rented out. In a place where the custom is not to, they are not rented out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'everything' adds a ברייתא about whether trees in a field are part of the rental.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's word 'everything' now covers more than farm work. It also covers what is included in the deal, here the fruit of the trees. Local custom decides that too.

phrases.english: To include what the Rabbis taught:

phrases.aramaic: מָקוֹם שֶׁנָּהֲגוּ לְהַשְׂכִּיר אִילָנוֹת עַל גַּבֵּי קַרְקַע –
phrases.english: A place where the custom is to rent out trees along with the land –
they are rented out;

phrases.aramaic: מָקוֹם שֶׁאֵין נָהֲגוּ לְהַשְׂכִּיר – אֵין מַשְׂכִּירִין.
phrases.english: a place where the custom is not to rent them out – they are not rented out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers what 'הכל' adds.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It adds the ברייתא that whether trees are included in a rental follows local custom.

steps.title: Isn't the first half of the ברייתא obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes 'where the custom is to rent them out, they are rented out' and asks why this needs to be said.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'A place where the custom is to rent out the trees – they are rented out.' Isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now looks at the ברייתא it just brought and asks why its first half needs to be said. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the custom is to include the trees, of course they are included. The גמרא is looking for a case where this is not so clear.

keyTerms.meaning: they rent out / the trees are included

phrases.english: A place where the custom is to rent them out, they are rented out –
It is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the first half of the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The first half of the ברייתא about renting out trees
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Following an existing custom seems too obvious to need saying.

steps.title: The owner who took a smaller share
steps.stepSummary: The line covers an owner who took only a quarter of the crop instead of the usual third. He might claim the lower share meant the trees were not included. The ברייתא teaches that he should have said so.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed where everyone gives out land for a third, and this owner gave it out for a quarter. You might think he can say: 'I lowered my share on the understanding that I would not give you the trees.' So the ברייתא teaches that he should have spelled it out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a case where the owner changed the usual split and silently meant that change to cancel the trees.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner gave the worker a better deal on the crop and thought this made up for leaving out the trees. Since he never said so, the custom wins and the worker gets the trees too.

phrases.aramaic: לָא צְרִיכָא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא יָהֲבִי בְּתִילְתָּא,
phrases.english: No, it is needed where everyone gives out land for a third,
phrases.notes: The numbers here are the owner's share of the crop.

phrases.english: and he went and gave it out for a quarter.
You might have said that he can say to him:
'When I took less for your sake,'
'it was on the understanding that I would not give you a share in the trees,'

phrases.aramaic: קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן דְּאִיבְּעִי לֵיהּ לְפָרוֹשֵׁי לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: it teaches us that he should have spelled it out to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא יָהֲבִי בְּתִילְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers why the first half of the ברייתא is needed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the line a new case where it is not obvious
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The owner's lower share might show that he meant to leave out the trees.
steps.terutzMaskana: The trees are still included, because he did not say so up front.

steps.title: Isn't the second half of the ברייתא obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes 'where the custom is not to rent them out, they are not rented out' and asks why this needs to be said.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'A place where the custom is not to rent out the trees – they are not rented out.' Isn't that obvious?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks the same question about the other half of the ברייתא. This sets up the matching answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the custom is the reverse: the trees are not included. Following that custom also seems too simple to need saying.

keyTerms.meaning: they do not rent out / the trees are not included

phrases.aramaic: מָקוֹם שֶׁנָּהֲגוּ שֶׁלֹּא לְהַשְׂכִּיר – אֵין מַשְׂכִּירִין.
phrases.english: A place where the custom is not to rent them out – they are not rented out.
It is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same question, now about the second half of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The second half of the ברייתא about not renting out trees
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Following an existing custom seems too obvious to need saying.

steps.title: The worker who gave a bigger share
steps.stepSummary: The line covers a worker who gave the owner a third instead of the usual quarter. He might claim the extra meant he would get the trees. The ברייתא teaches that he should have said so.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed where everyone takes land for a quarter, and this worker took it for a third. You might think he can say: 'I gave you more on the understanding that you would give me the trees.' So the ברייתא teaches that he should have spelled it out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the mirror image of the last case. This time the worker pays extra and silently expects the trees in return.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the worker gave the owner a better deal and thought it bought him the fruit of the trees. Since he never said so, the custom wins and he gets no trees.
steps.whatToRemember: In all three cases (plowing, the owner's lower share, the worker's higher share), local custom decides the deal. If someone wants something different, he has to say it clearly at the start. A silent intention, even one backed by a changed price, doesn't count.
steps.confusionAlert: Steps 11 and 13 are mirror images. In step 11 the owner gives up part of his share and hopes to keep the trees. In step 13 the worker adds to the owner's share and hopes to get the trees. Either way, custom wins.

phrases.aramaic: לָא צְרִיכָא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא מְקַבְּלִי בְּרִיבְעָא,
phrases.english: No, it is needed where everyone takes on land for a quarter,
and he went and took it on for a third.
You might have said that he can say to him:
'When I gave you more,'
'it was on the understanding that you would give me a share in the trees,'

phrases.aramaic: קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן דְּאִיבְּעִי לֵיהּ לְפָרוֹשֵׁי לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: it teaches us that he should have spelled it out to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא מְקַבְּלִי בְּרִיבְעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 12 using the same pattern as step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the line a new case where it is not obvious
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The worker's higher payment might show that he meant to get the trees.
steps.terutzMaskana: He does not get the trees, because he did not say so up front.

steps.title: The straw is shared just like the grain
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: the owner and the אריס share the straw and stubble the same way they share the grain.
steps.simpleTranslation: Just as they divide the grain, so they divide the straw and the stubble.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה so it can comment on it. This sets up רב יוסף's remark in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The deal between the owner and the אריס is not only about the main crop. Whatever share each side gets of the grain, he gets the same share of the leftover straw and stubble.

phrases.english: Just as they divide the grain
so they divide the straw and the stubble.
phrases.notes: 'They' means the field owner and the worker who farms it for a share.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the ברייתא about trees to the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The straw and stubble are shared in the same proportion as the grain.

steps.title: In Babylonia the worker does not get straw
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף reports that in בבל the custom is not to give straw to the אריס.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: In Babylonia they are accustomed not to give straw to the sharecropper.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף adds a local fact: in בבל, the owner keeps all the straw.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's rule follows local custom. In בבל the custom is different, so there the אריס gets a share of the grain but no straw.

keyTerms.meaning: They are accustomed; it is the custom
The sharecropper, who farms a field for a share of the crop

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
In Babylonia they are accustomed
not to give straw to the sharecropper.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a local exception to the משנה's rule about straw.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In בבל the custom is that the אריס gets no straw.

steps.title: Why does it matter to state this custom?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference רב יוסף's report makes.
steps.simpleTranslation: What difference does it make?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רב יוסף needed to tell us this custom. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If everyone in בבל already follows this custom, why say it out loud? The גמרא wants a case where knowing the custom actually changes the outcome.

keyTerms.meaning: What practical difference does it make?

phrases.english: What difference does it make?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks why רב יוסף's statement is needed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A practical case where knowing the Babylonian custom matters.

steps.title: An owner who gives straw is just being generous
steps.stepSummary: If some owner in בבל does give straw, that is his own generosity. We do not treat it as the custom.
steps.simpleTranslation: That if there is a person who does give straw, he is generous, and we do not learn from him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: the custom tells us how to judge an owner who does give straw.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might see an owner giving straw and think that this is the real custom. רב יוסף teaches that the custom is set: no straw. One kind owner's gift is a favor, not a rule other workers can demand.

keyTerms.meaning: We learn; we draw a rule from it

phrases.english: That if there is a person who does give,
he is being generous,
phrases.notes: Literally 'he has a good eye', a common way of saying someone gives with a generous heart.

phrases.english: and we do not learn from him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 16.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The custom keeps one generous owner from changing what other workers are owed.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows a key rule about custom: one person's extra kindness does not create a new custom for everyone.

steps.title: Who builds the field's fence
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף rules that the layers of the earth wall and the poles for the thorn fence are the owner's job. Building the thorn fence itself is the אריס's job.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: The first, second and third layers of the wall, and the poles for the thorn fence, are the owner's job. The thorn fence itself is the sharecropper's job.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף divides the work of fencing the field between the owner and the אריס.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The heavy, lasting parts of the fence fall on the בעל הבית: the earth wall and the poles. The lighter work of weaving the thorn fence falls on the worker.

keyTerms.meaning: The first, second and third layers of the earth wall around the field

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
The first, second, and third layers of the wall
phrases.notes: These three words name the layers of the earth wall that fences in the field.

phrases.english: and the poles for the thorn fence
are the owner's job,
but the thorn fence itself is the sharecropper's job.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: בּוּכְרָא וְטָפְתָא וְאַרְכַּבְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ruling by רב יוסף about who does which jobs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The earth wall and the fence poles are on the owner. The thorn fence is on the אריס.

steps.title: The general rule for fencing
steps.stepSummary: The main fence belongs to the owner. Any extra protection belongs to the אריס.
steps.simpleTranslation: The general rule of the matter: the whole main fence is the owner's job, and extra guarding is the sharecropper's job.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sums up רב יוסף's fence ruling as one simple rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of a list, we now have the idea behind it. The basic boundary of the field is the owner's duty. Anything added for extra safety is the worker's duty.

keyTerms.meaning: The general rule of the matter
The fence or boundary of the field

steps.whatToRemember: Main fence = owner. Extra protection = אריס.

phrases.english: The general rule of the matter:
the whole main fence is the owner's job;
extra guarding is the sharecropper's job.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the list in step 18 into one general rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The main boundary is on the owner. Extra protection is on the worker.

steps.title: Tools come from the owner, channels from the worker
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף rules that the owner supplies the hoe, basket, bucket and irrigation device. The אריס digs the irrigation channels.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב יוסף said: The hoe, the basket, the bucket and the irrigation device are the owner's to supply. The sharecropper makes the irrigation channels.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף gives another split: who supplies the tools and who does the digging.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The equipment is a cost that stays with the field, so the בעל הבית provides it. The work of digging the water channels is labor, so it falls on the אריס.

keyTerms.meaning: A device for raising water to irrigate

phrases.english: And Rav Yosef said:
The hoe and the basket
and the bucket and the irrigation device
are the owner's to supply;
the sharecropper makes the irrigation channels.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another ruling by רב יוסף on dividing duties.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The owner supplies the tools. The אריס digs the channels.

steps.title: Vine branches and poles are shared like the wine
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: just as the two sides share the wine, they share the vine branches and the poles.
steps.simpleTranslation: Just as they divide the wine, so they divide the vine branches and the poles.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה, this time about a vineyard. This sets up the question about the 'poles'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same idea as the straw rule. The side products of a vineyard are shared in the same way as the main product, the wine.

phrases.english: Just as they divide the wine
so they divide the vine branches and the poles.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the משנה for its next line.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Vine branches and poles are shared like the wine.

steps.title: What are these poles for?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the poles in the משנה are used for.
steps.simpleTranslation: Poles: what are they for?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what kind of poles the משנה means. This sets up the answer from the school of רבי ינאי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A vineyard does not obviously produce 'poles', so the גמרא wants to know which poles the משנה is talking about.

keyTerms.meaning: What are they for? What is their use?

phrases.english: Poles: what are they for?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what a word in the משנה refers to.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the 'poles' in the משנה are and what they are used for.

steps.title: Split poles that hold up the vines
steps.stepSummary: The school of רבי ינאי explains that these are split poles used to prop up the vines.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said in the school of רבי ינאי: These are split poles, which are used to hold up the vines.
steps.whatsHappening: The answer: the poles are split canes that support the vines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now we know what is being shared. It is the supports that hold the vines upright, not some crop that grows in the vineyard.

keyTerms.meaning: They hold up or prop up

phrases.english: They said in the school of Rabbi Yannai:
split poles,
with which they hold up the vines.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The poles are split canes that support the vines.

steps.title: Why say that both supply the poles?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's line that both sides supply the poles, and asks why it needs to say this.
steps.simpleTranslation: And both of them supply the poles. Why do I need this?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges this line of the משנה as unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה already said that both sides share the poles. Adding that both supply them seems to add nothing, so the גמרא asks why it is there.

phrases.english: And both of them supply the poles.
Why do I need this?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּשְׁנֵיהֶם מְסַפְּקִין אֶת הַקָּנִים. לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next line of the משנה and questions why it is needed.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's words 'both of them supply the poles'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: After 'they share the poles', saying 'both supply them' looks like an extra line that teaches nothing new.

steps.title: The line gives the reason for sharing
steps.stepSummary: The משנה is explaining its reason: both sides share the poles because both sides supplied them.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is giving the reason: Why do both divide the poles? Because both of them supply the poles.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that this line is not a new rule. It is the reason behind the rule before it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Read the two lines together: they share the poles because they both paid for them. So the line is not extra. It explains why the sharing is fair.
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's 'both supply the poles' is the reason for 'both share the poles', not a separate rule.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read this as two separate rules. The second line explains the first.

phrases.english: It is saying 'what is the reason':
what is the reason both divide the poles?
Because both of them supply the poles.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereads the line as the reason for the rule, not a new rule.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The line seemed to be an extra, unneeded rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: The line explains why the poles are shared: both sides supplied them.

steps.title: Tenant pays full rent even if the spring dries up or the trees are cut down
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה rules that a tenant who rented an irrigated field or a field of trees does not pay less rent if the spring dries up or the trees are cut down.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Someone rented a field from his friend, and it was an irrigated field or a field with trees. Then the spring dried up or the trees were cut down. He does not take anything off his rent.
steps.whatsHappening: A brand new משנה starts here. It gives the basic rule: losing the water or the trees does not lower the tenant's rent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The tenant here is a חוכר, who promised the owner a fixed amount of produce as rent. The משנה says that even though the field lost the very thing that made it valuable, he must still pay the full amount. The second half of the משנה will show when this changes.

keyTerms.meaning: One who takes on a field from its owner to work it
An irrigated field, watered by a spring or channel
His fixed rent, paid in produce

phrases.english: MISHNA:
One who receives a field from his fellow
and it is an irrigated field,
or a field of trees,
if the spring dried up or the trees were cut down,
he does not subtract for him from his rent.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה. It moves on from the earlier discussion about sharing wine, branches and poles.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the field's spring dries up or its trees are cut down, the tenant pays his full rent.

steps.title: If he rented it by name as an irrigated or tree field, he pays less
steps.stepSummary: The משנה continues: if the tenant said 'Lease me this irrigated field' or 'this field of trees,' and the water or trees were lost, he may pay less rent.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he said to the owner, 'Rent me this irrigated field' or 'this field of trees,' and then the spring dried up or the trees were cut down, he takes it off his rent.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the opposite ruling for a different case. Here the tenant named the water or the trees in the rental deal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: What changes is the wording of the deal. When the tenant rented the field by name as 'an irrigated field' or 'a field of trees,' the water or trees became part of what he was renting. So when they are gone, he is not getting what he rented, and his rent goes down.

keyTerms.meaning: Lease me, rent to me (for a fixed payment)

steps.whatToRemember: Same field, different result: just renting a field means full rent. Renting it by name as 'this irrigated field' or 'this tree field' means the rent goes down when the water or trees are lost.

phrases.english: If he said to him:
phrases.notes: The tenant is speaking to the landowner.

phrases.english: "Lease me this irrigated field"
or "this field of trees,"
and the spring dried up or the trees were cut down,
he subtracts for him from his rent.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם אָמַר לוֹ: חֲכוֹר לִי שָׂדֶה בֵּית הַשְּׁלָחִין זוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite case to step 26. The difference is how the rental was worded.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the tenant rented the field by name as 'this irrigated field' or 'this field of trees,' he may lower his rent when the water or trees are lost.

steps.title: What exact case is the משנה talking about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens by asking what the exact situation in the משנה's first ruling is.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: What is the case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the exact case behind the משנה's first ruling. This short question sets up the next step, where the גמרא tries out a possible answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה just said 'the spring dried up' without saying what kind of water source it was. The גמרא wants to know exactly which water source dried up, because the answer may change the ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What does it look like?

phrases.english: GEMARA: What are the circumstances?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The גמרא begins discussing the משנה from step 26.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What kind of water source dried up in the משנה's case where the tenant still pays full rent.

steps.title: It can't mean the big river dried up, since that is a disaster for the whole area
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the big main river dried up, then rejects this. That would be a מכת מדינה, so the tenant should get to pay less.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say the big river dried up, why can't he take it off his rent? He should be able to tell the owner, 'This is a disaster for the whole area!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries one possible case, that the big river dried up. It quickly shows why this cannot be what the משנה means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A big river waters the whole region, so if it dries up, everyone is hurt. That is a מכת מדינה, a disaster that hits the whole area, and in that kind of case the tenant does get to pay less. Since the משנה says he does not pay less, it cannot be talking about the big river.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (a suggestion the גמרא is about to reject)
A disaster that hits the whole area

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not asking 'why not?' because it is unsure. It means: if this were a big river, the tenant would clearly win, so the משנה must mean something else.

phrases.english: If we say that the large river dried up,

phrases.aramaic: אַמַּאי אֵינוֹ מְנַכֶּה לוֹ מִן חֲכוֹרוֹ?
phrases.english: why does he not subtract from his rent?
Let him say to him: It is a regional disaster!
phrases.notes: The tenant would be saying this to the landowner.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries a first answer to the question in step 28, then rejects it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the משנה's dried-up spring means the big river.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the big river dried up, it is a מכת מדינה, and then the tenant does pay less. That goes against the משנה's ruling that he pays full rent.

steps.title: רב פפא: The case is a small river that dried up
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that the משנה means a small river, one that waters only this field. He then starts to give the landowner's argument.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: It is where a small river dried up, because the owner can say to him:
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives the real case: a small river dried up, not the big one. He begins to quote what the landowner can say to the tenant, and the quote continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A small river that waters only this field is not a disaster for the whole area. Only this one field lost its water. So the tenant cannot claim a מכת מדינה, and the משנה's ruling that he pays full rent makes sense. The landowner's exact words come next.

keyTerms.meaning: A small river (waters only this field)
Because he can say to him

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
Where a small river dried up,
as he can say to him:
phrases.notes: The landowner is speaking to the tenant. His words continue right after this.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: דִּיבַשׁ נַהֲרָא זוּטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 28 after the big-river suggestion was rejected in step 29.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה means a small river that waters only this field dried up. That is not a מכת מדינה, so the tenant must pay full rent.
